title: The ancient Scriptures call us to wisdom
source_text: Ὅτι δὲ βούλεται ἡμᾶς εἶναι σοφοὺς ὁ λόγος, δεικτέον καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν παλαιῶν καὶ Ἰουδαϊκῶν γραμμάτων. οἷς καὶ ἡμεῖς χρώμεθα· οὐχ ἧττον δὲ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν μετὰ τὸν Ἰησοῦν γραφέντων καὶ ἐν ταῖς ἐκκλησίαις θείων εἶναι πεπιστευμένων. ἀναγέγραπται δὴ ἐν πεντηκοστῷ ψαλμῷ Δαυὶδ ἐν τῇ πρὸς θεὸν εὐχῇ λέγων· „τὰ ἄδηλα καὶ τὰ κρύφια τῆς σοφίας σου ἐδήλωσάς μοι.“ καὶ εἴ τις γε ἐντύχοι τοῖς ψαλμοῖς. εὕροι ἂν πολλῶν καὶ σοφῶν δογμάτων πλήρη τὴν βίβλον. καὶ Σολομὼν δὲ. ἐπεὶ σοφίαν ᾔτησεν, ἀπεδέχθη· καὶ τῆς σοφίας αὐτοῦ τὰ ἴχνη ἔστιν ἐν τοῖς συγγράμμασι θεωρῆσαι, μεγάλην ἔχοντα ἐν βραχυλογίᾳ περίνοιαν· ἐν οἷς ἂν εὕροις πολλὰ ἐγκώμια τῆς σοφίας καὶ προτρεπτικὰ περὶ τοῦ σοφίαν δεῖν ἀναλαβεῖν. καὶ οὕτω γε σοφὸς ην Σολομὼν. ὥστε τὴν βασιλίδα Σαβὰ, ἀκούσασαν αὐτοῦ „τὸ ὄνομα“ „καὶ τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου,“ ἐλθεῖν „πειράσαι αὐτὸν ἐν αἰνίγμασιν.“ ἥτις „καὶ ἐλάλησεν αὐτῷ πάντα, ὅσα ἦν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτῆς. καὶ ἀπήγγειλεν αὐτῇ Σολομὼν πάντας τοὺς λόγους αὐτῆς· οὐκ ἦν λόγος παρεωραμένος ὑπὸ τοῦ βασιλέως, ὃν οὐκ ἀπήγγειλεν αὐτῇ. καὶ εἶδε βασίλισσα Σαβὰ πᾶσαν φρόνησιν Σολομὼν“ καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ αὐτόν· „καὶ ἐξ αὑτῆς ἐγένετο. καὶ εἶπε πρὸς τὸν βασιλέα· ἀληθὴς ὁ λόγος. ὃν ἤκουσα ἐν τῇ γῇ μου περὶ σοῦ καὶ περὶ τῆς φρονήσεώς σου· καὶ οὐκ ἐπίστευσα τοῖς λαλοῦσί μοι, ἕως ὅτε παρεγενόμην καὶ ἑωράκασιν οἱ ὀφθαλμοί μου· καὶ ἰδοὺ οὐκ ἔστι καθὼς ἀπήγγειλάν μοι τὸ ἥμισυ. προστέθεικας σοφίαν καὶ ἀγαθὰ πρὸς αὐτὰ ἐπὶ πᾶσαν τὴν ἀκοὴν. ἣν ἤκουσα.“ γέγραπται δὴ περὶ (τοῦ) αὐτοῦ ὅτι „καὶ ἔδωκε κύριος φρόνησιν τῷ Σολομὼν καὶ σοφίαν πολλὴν σφόδρα καὶ χύμα καρδίας ὡς ἡ ἄμμος ἡ παρὰ τὴν θάλασσαν. καὶ ἐπληθύνθη σοφία ἐν Σολομὼν σφόδρα ὑπὲρ τὴν φρόνησιν πάντων ἀρχαίων καὶ ὑπὲρ πάντας φρονίμους Αἰγύπτου. καὶ ἐσοφίσατο ὑπὲρ πάντας ἀνθρώπους, καὶ ἐσοφίσατο ὑπὲρ Γεθὰν τὸν Ἐζαρίτην καὶ τὸν Ἐμὰδ καὶ τὸν Χαλκαδὶ καὶ Ἀραδὰ. υἱοὺς Μάδ· καὶ ἦν ὀνομαστὸς ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς ἔθνεσι κύκλῳ. καὶ ἐλάλησε Σολομὼν τρισχιλίας παραβολὰς, καὶ ἦσαν ᾠδαὶ αὐτοῦ πεντακισχίλιαι. καὶ ἐλάλησεν περὶ τῶν ξύλων ἀπὸ τῆς κέδρου τῆς ἐν τῷ Λιβάνῳ καὶ ἕως τῆς ὑσσώπου τῆς ἐκπορευομένης διὰ τοῦ τοίχου. καὶ ἐλάλησε περὶ τῶν ἰχθύων καὶ τῶν κτηνῶν· καὶ παρεγίνοντο πάντες οἱ λαοὶ ἀκοῦσαι τῆς σοφίας Σολομῶντος· καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς. οἵ ἤκουον τῆς σοφίας αὐτοῦ.“ οὕτω δὲ βούλεται σοφοὺς εἶναι ἐν τοῖς πιστεύουσιν ὁ λόγος, ὥστε ὑπὲρ τοῦ γυμνάσαι τὴν σύνεσιν τῶν ἀκουόντων τὰ μὲν (ἐν) αἰνίγμασι τὰ δὲ ἐν τοῖς καλουμένοις σκοτεινοῖς λόγοις λελαληκέναι τὰ δὲ διὰ παραβολῶν καὶ ἄλλα διὰ προβλημάτων. καί φησι γέ τις τῶν προφητῶν, ὁ Ὠσηὲ. ἐπὶ τέλει τῶν λόγων ἑαυτοῦ· „τίς σοφὸς καὶ συνήσει ταῦτα; ἢ συνετὸς καὶ ἐπιγνώσεται αὐτά;“ Δανιὴλ δὲ καὶ οἱ μετ᾿ αὐτοῦ αἰχμαλωτισθέντες τοσοῦτον προέκοψαν καὶ ἐν τοῖς μαθήμασιν. ἅτινα ἤσκουν ἐν Βαβυλῶνι οἱ περὶ τὸν βασιλέα σοφοὶ, ὡς πάντων αὐτῶν διαφέροντας ἀποδειχθῆναι τούτους „δεκαπλασίως.“ λέγεται δὲ (καὶ) ἐν τῷ Ἰεζεκιὴλ πρὸς τὸν Τύρου ἄρχοντα, μέγα φρονοῦντα ἐπὶ σοφίᾳ· „μὴ σὺ σοφώτερος εἶ τοῦ Δανιήλ; πᾶν κρύφιον οὐκ ἐπεδείχθη σοι;“
pass_a_gloss: That the word (λόγος) wishes (βούλομαι) us to be wise (σοφός), [it] must be shown (δεικτέον) both from the ancient (παλαιός) and Jewish writings (γράμματα), which we too use (χράομαι), and no less from those written after Jesus and believed (πιστεύω) in the churches (ἐκκλησίαι) to be divine (θεῖος). It is recorded (ἀναγράφω) in the fiftieth psalm (ψαλμός), David saying in the prayer (εὐχή) to God: ‘the unclear (ἄδηλα) and hidden (κρύφια) [things] of your wisdom you made clear (δηλόω) to me.’ And if anyone meets with (ἐντυγχάνω, reads) the psalms, he would find the book (βίβλος) full of many and wise doctrines (δόγματα). And Solomon, since he asked (αἰτέω) wisdom, was accepted (ἀποδέχομαι); and of his wisdom the traces (ἴχνη) it is possible to behold (θεωρέω) in the writings (συγγράμματα), having great circumspection/depth of thought (περίνοια) in brevity of speech (βραχυλογία); in which you would find many praises (ἐγκώμια) of wisdom and exhortations (προτρεπτικά) about needing to take up (ἀναλαμβάνω) wisdom. And so wise was Solomon that the queen (βασιλίς) of Saba, having heard ‘his name’ ‘and the name of the Lord (κύριος),’ came ‘to test (πειράζω) him in riddles (αἰνίγματα)’; who ‘also spoke to him all, as many as were in her heart, and Solomon reported (ἀπαγγέλλω) to her all her words; there was not a word overlooked (παροράω) by the king which he did not report to her. And the queen of Saba saw all the understanding (φρόνησις) of Solomon’ and the [things] about him: ‘and she became out of herself (ἐξ ἑαυτῆς γίγνομαι), and said to the king: True (ἀληθής) the word which I heard in my land about you and about your understanding; and I did not believe those speaking to me until I came and my eyes have seen; and behold, it is not as they reported to me, the half (ἥμισυ). You have added (προστίθημι) wisdom and good things to them beyond all the hearing (ἀκοή, report) which I heard.’ It is written about him that ‘and the Lord gave understanding to Solomon and wisdom very much and outpouring/breadth of heart (χύμα καρδίας) as the sand beside the sea; and wisdom was multiplied (πληθύνω) in Solomon exceedingly beyond the understanding of all ancients and beyond all prudent of Egypt; and he became wise (σοφίζομαι) beyond all men, and was wise beyond Gethan the Ezarite and Emad and Chalcadi and Arada, sons of Mad; and he was named (ὀνομαστός) among all the nations around. And Solomon spoke three thousand parables (παραβολαί), and his songs (ᾠδαί) were five thousand. And he spoke about the trees (ξύλα) from the cedar in Lebanon even to the hyssop going out through the wall; and he spoke about the fishes and the beasts (κτήνη); and all the peoples came to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and about/from all the kings of the earth, who heard of his wisdom.’ So the word wishes there to be wise [men] among those who believe that, for the sake of exercising (γυμνάζω) the understanding (σύνεσις) of the hearers, it has spoken some [things] in riddles, some in the so-called dark (σκοτεινοί) sayings, some through parables, and others through problems (προβλήματα). And one of the prophets, Hosea, says at the end of his words: ‘Who [is] wise and will understand (συνίημι) these things? Or intelligent (συνετός) and will recognise (ἐπιγινώσκω) them?’ And Daniel and those taken captive (αἰχμαλωτίζω) with him advanced (προκόπτω) so much also in the learnings (μαθήματα) which the wise [men] around the king practised (ἀσκέω) in Babylon, that these were shown (ἀποδείκνυμι) to surpass (διαφέρω) them all ‘tenfold’ (δεκαπλασίως). And it is said also in Ezekiel to the ruler (ἄρχων) of Tyre, thinking big (μέγα φρονέω) on wisdom: ‘Are you wiser than Daniel? Every secret (κρύφιον) was not shown (ἐπιδείκνυμι) to you?’
pass_b_english: That our teaching wants us to be wise must be shown both from the ancient Jewish writings, which we also use, and no less from those written after Jesus and believed in the churches to be divine. It is written in the fiftieth Psalm that David, in his prayer to God, says: “You have made plain to me the hidden and secret things of your wisdom” (Psalm 51:6). Indeed, anyone who reads the Psalms would find the book full of many wise doctrines. Solomon too was approved because he asked for wisdom (1 Kings 3:9–12; 2 Chronicles 1:10–12); and in his writings one can see the traces of his wisdom, which hold great depth of thought in few words. In them you would find many praises of wisdom and many exhortations to take up wisdom.

So wise indeed was Solomon that the queen of Sheba, when she heard “his name” “and the name of the Lord,” came “to test him with riddles” (1 Kings 10:1). She “spoke to him all that was in her heart, and Solomon explained to her all her words; there was not a word passed over by the king that he did not explain to her. And the queen of Sheba saw all the understanding of Solomon” (1 Kings 10:2–4) and all that belonged to him; “and she was beside herself, and she said to the king, ‘True was the report that I heard in my own land about you and about your understanding; and I did not believe those who told me until I came and my eyes had seen; and see, they did not tell me the half. You have added wisdom and good things to them beyond all the report that I heard’ ” (1 Kings 10:5–7).

It is written of him that “the Lord gave Solomon understanding and very great wisdom, and largeness of heart like the sand that is beside the sea. And wisdom was multiplied in Solomon exceedingly, beyond the understanding of all the ancients and beyond all the wise men of Egypt. And he was wiser than all men, and wiser than Gethan the Ezarite, and Emad, and Chalcadi, and Arada, the sons of Mad; and he was renowned among all the nations round about. And Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs were five thousand. And he spoke of the trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out through the wall; and he spoke of the fishes and the beasts. And all the peoples came to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and from all the kings of the earth, who heard of his wisdom” (1 Kings 4:29–34).

Our teaching so wants there to be wise men among believers that, to exercise the understanding of its hearers, it has spoken some things in riddles, some in what are called dark sayings (Proverbs 1:6), some through parables, and others through puzzles. And one of the prophets, Hosea, says at the end of his words: “Who is wise, and will understand these things? Or who is prudent, and will know them?” (Hosea 14:9). Daniel, and those who were taken captive with him, made such progress even in the learning practised in Babylon by the wise men around the king that they were shown to surpass them all “tenfold” (Daniel 1:20). And in Ezekiel it is said to the ruler of Tyre, who prided himself greatly on his wisdom: “Are you wiser than Daniel? Has not every secret been shown to you?” (Ezekiel 28:3).

choices.choice: LXX renumbering: ‘the fiftieth Psalm’ is kept as Origen says it; LXX Psalm 50:8 = English Psalm 51:6. 1 Kings is 3 Kingdoms in the LXX; the long quotation ‘the Lord gave Solomon understanding …’ is LXX 3 Kingdoms 5:9–14, which is 1 Kings 4:29–34 in English Bibles (Hebrew 5:9–14). The names follow the Greek as staged (Gethan the Ezarite, Emad, Chalcadi, Arada, sons of Mad); English Bibles have Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol and Darda, sons of Mahol. Origen's quotation abbreviates the list of what Solomon spoke about (fishes and beasts only). The last clause reads καὶ περὶ πάντων τῶν βασιλέων τῆς γῆς; the LXX has παρά (‘from all the kings’), and I rendered by that sense (‘and from all the kings of the earth’), since περί (‘about’) gives no clear sense here; possible copying error. Σαβά rendered ‘Sheba’, the usual English form. καὶ τὰ κατ᾿ αὐτόν (‘and the things about him’) stands outside the quotation marks: Origen's own summary of 1 Kings 10:4b–5a (his house, table and servants), which he skips. ‘was approved’ (ἀπεδέχθη) for Solomon's request alludes to 1 Kings 3:9–12 (compare 2 Chronicles 1:10–12). ‘traces of his wisdom in his writings’ and ‘praises of wisdom’ refer to Proverbs and the other Solomonic books in general; no single verse is cited. ‘riddles … dark sayings … parables’ echoes Proverbs 1:6 (LXX παραβολὴν καὶ σκοτεινὸν λόγον … αἰνίγματα), cited inline; προβλήματα (‘puzzles’) may also echo LXX Psalm 77:2 (English 78:2), uncited as uncertain. Hosea 14:9 English = LXX/Hebrew 14:10. Ezekiel 28:3: Origen's second question (πᾶν κρύφιον οὐκ ἐπεδείχθη σοι;) does not match the common LXX wording (σοφοὶ οὐκ ἐπαίδευσάν σε …) and stands nearer the Hebrew (‘no secret is hidden from you’); translated as Origen gives it. The supplements (ἐν), (τοῦ) and (καὶ) are translated or have no effect on the English. ὁ λόγος rendered ‘our teaching’. Reviewer: μεγάλην ἔχοντα (neuter plural) agrees with τὰ ἴχνη, not with the dative συγγράμμασι, so it is the traces of wisdom that hold great depth in few words. 2 Chronicles 1:10–12 added beside 1 Kings 3:9–12 because only Chronicles has Solomon ask in so many words for ‘wisdom’ (σοφίαν). χύμα καρδίας (an outpouring or abundance of heart; the LXX has πλάτος) rendered ‘largeness of heart’. ἀπήγγειλεν rendered ‘explained’ (declared to her), which reads more clearly than ‘told her all her words’.
